item.title: Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too. Read more
item.description:
Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too.
Gears of War: E-Day could very easily have been a rote prequel, the kind of thing that asks questions no-one particularly cares about. We were, after all, introduced to the doomed planet of Sera in 2006's ground-breaking first Gears of War title. But the only thing ground-breaking in E-Day is, well, quite literally the ground: that eponymous 'E' stands for 'Emergence', since E-Day takes us back to the very beginning, when the antagonistic Locust first started crawling out of their holes to wreak havoc on humanity.
That's not a criticism, per se. I think E-Day is excellent at what it does: it's a cover shooter with Tarantino-esque comedy violence barely held together by a plot that falls apart like so much Locust viscera if you examine it for more than five minutes. But - as I said in my campaign review - that's fun. That's fine. I don't come to Gears for Hugo Award-level narrative conceit, I come for wet headshots, arcade cover shooting, and chainsaw guns that go brrr.
And, by that metric, the game is awesome. I won't retread too much ground talking about the campaign here (which is a somewhat ironic statement, as the game makes you go back-and-forth over the same bridge no less than three times throughout the course of the campaign), and instead I will let that form one pillar of the overall E-Day experience. The other two are 'Versus' and 'Horde Siege' - and I'm starting with the latter, because I think that's the real, exposed heart of Gears.
Horde has been a fixture of the series since it was introduced in Gears of War 2 (2008), where it was a fairly barebones affair: fend off 50 waves of increasingly pissed-off enemies, survive. It's Gears' take on CoD Zombies, effectively, and has been present in every game since - with varying levels of success along the way. But E-Day's reinterpretation of the mode outshines them all, despite a convoluted on-boarding and some janky UI. Instead of four player-teams (or five, for some reason, Gears 5), E-Day teams you up with 11 others, breaking you off into units of four players each. The maps in the mode are taken from the open-ended areas in the campaign - which justifies their existence, since I found them aggravating and a bit pointless in the story mode - and feature multiple objectives.
You know what it reminds me of? Destiny. With multiple 'fireteams' zipping around the map and completing their own objectives, whilst simultaneously dropping in to help other squads here and there, it generates this slightly buzzy, frantic energy - especially when a Corpser or Brumak tunnels up out of nowhere and suddenly all 12 players are forced into repelling this behemoth threat before they can realistically continue with their own missions. Each squad gets to choose its own difficulty, and that scales damage dealt and received to your team. It's possible to have a squad playing 'Allfather' difficulty whilst another is on 'Rookie', and you're both trying to take down the same cursed spider-bastard at once, but having a very different experience in tandem. It's a bit of engineering wizardry that can be activated in Campaign, too. Shout out to Kate Rayner, longstanding Coalition technical director, because she and her team have managed to employ all those Unreal 5 dials and levers in an artisanal way here.
The process is gamified by 'energy' drops; the more energy you have, the more weapons, ammo, defensive installations, or squad upgrades you can buy. You choose a class before deployment, and then you can spend your 'energy' to kit yourself out more as the siege continues. There have been so many emergent moments in my 15 hours of playing this mode, I'm a little taken aback. The highlight was running to my extraction point after clearing our group's objective, seeing another squad nearly get wiped by a minigun-toting Grinder, and landing a perfect headshot to splatter its brains all over the concrete. A slide, a roll, and I revive one ally. A hop over some low cover and I've got another. A tight corner swat turn gets me the third. I then 'roadie run' to the chopper with one second left before extraction, whilst my own fireteam covers my ass with suppressing fire from the helicopter. "Enjoy the ride, Gears," the game prompts me, as my watch tells me I've entered a 'cardio' session.
I've not experienced such multiplayer synergy since my Destiny 2 days; it's enough to keep me playing into the future. I think Gears will remain on my harddrive just for Horde Siege, if I'm honest - there's no better way of blowing off steam after a rough day than teaming up with a group of randos (yep, the matchmaking is solid) and popping Locust heads. Between the level design - or is it urban planning? - and three-tier cover mechanics, Versus and Siege feel fresh enough compared to past Gears games to be worth investigating (even if you thought all this juvenile musclebound bloodletting was behind you).
I've never thought so much about a jump button in all my life. Gears, it turns out, really needed one. It sounds small fry, but cover shooters are always such a drag when the clunky controls force you into certain death: in the 360 games, it always felt like you were moving digital characters around an analogue world - Marcus moved like a rook on a chessboard but the floor was actually just real ground all along. E-Day makes everyone more acrobatic - maybe it's because they're not quite Rob Liefeld-esque steroid-addled abominations at this point - which makes climbing or mantling over cover more intuitive. Slides and rolls glue you to cover that's actually quite far away, which makes everything feel more cinematic and intentional. And even incendiary grenades, emulsion-powered shotguns and other fancy wares make cover-swapping an integral part of the strategy: you can't camp, in any mode, otherwise you're going to get skewered.
Which brings us to Versus. Gears PvP was always either Very Fun or Very Annoying, depending on how well you're doing. But that binary has been offset by these new acrobatic Gears you find yourself controlling - leaping over insta-death pits is exhilarating. Moreso if you land and charge up your Torque Bow to land an insta-kill headshot on an unsuspecting greenhorn cowering in fear across the gap. And even more so if the bolt that pierced the rookie's head then lands in the leg of a seasoned vet who runs into his teammate and explodes them both. That, right there, is uniquely Gears.
The flip side is, of course, when it happens to you. Or when you encounter a sweaty tryhard 'wall-bouncer' that manages to wipe your squad in seconds. Or when you mistime a jump and fall into an instadeath pit. Or when you run out of ammo whilst defending a 'king of the hill' flavoured objective and find yourself using a disgusting gun you've touched exactly once in the past 35 hours of playtime. It's part of the experience, sure, but… eurgh. 'Back to Horde Siege', I mutter, as chunks of my skull decorate xX_yourmum69_Xx's shop-bought premium skin.
The same tidal nature present in Campaign maps onto the rest of the E-Day package: for everything I want to celebrate, there's something that just about undercuts it. Horde Siege is a phenomenal interpretation of the Gears formula, but the UI, onboarding and pacing is a little wonky. Versus is a tight, focused exploration of PvP cover-shooting, but there are balance and mechanical issues that make it hard for more casual players to enjoy. The Campaign is pacy and well-designed and fun, but with baffling checkpoints and a couple of repetitive beats.
Gears of War: E-Day is a game of contrasts: conservative by its very nature, but with enough technical proficiency and iterative thinking to make its old-fashioned ideas feel competent and engaging. Bleeding edge graphics with 20-year-old design sensibilities drip into this bloody crucible of familiarity that does nostalgia right. It's telling that a successful Xbox exclusive looks the same in 2026 as it did in 2006, but that isn't a mark against The Coalition and the retro-modern chimera its spawned here - this beast stands proudly on its own two feet, as a living example of how you appeal to a generation of gamers that had its cake and ate it. And that's no mean feat.
A copy of Gears of War E-Day was provided for this review by Xbox.

item.title: British actor Charlie Cox, best known for being Daredevil in Marvel's Netflix series - but known closer to home as the voice of Gustav in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 - has said he's just finished recording for a Sega game which hasn't been announced yet. Read more
item.description:
British actor Charlie Cox, best known for being Daredevil in Marvel's Netflix series - but known closer to home as the voice of Gustav in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 - has said he's just finished recording for a Sega game which hasn't been announced yet.
Cox, speaking to IGN at New York Comic-Con 2026, said: "I did another one! It doesn't have a name yet. I did a Sega one. It hasn't come out yet. It was fun to do. It's hard. It's a whole different job, man."
He added: "I'm not sure what I'm allowed to say but I showed up for it, and [when] I met them for the first time, they asked me to do this game, and so I agreed to it. Then I had to do 40 hours or whatever it was, and I showed up for the first day, and I was like, 'Hi guys, nice to meet you! How are you?' And all of them went, '...oh, he's English.' They'd hoped, they’d wanted him to be American. But now I've got to do 40 hours of lines I've not prepared in an accent."
Cox said earlier this year that Clair Obscur had "opened a new avenue for my professional work", and that he was going to be recording for a new game this year, though he didn't say which one. Presumably, this Sega game was it. But what could it be?
Sega's big upcoming release, in January 2027, is Stranger than Heaven, which has already unveiled bizarre cameo roles for megastars Snoop Dogg and the late Tupac Shakur. But this game has been known about for a while and it's late in the day for Cox to be recording so much dialogue for it.
Could Cox have a role in Total War: Warhammer 40K? Stranger Things star David Harbour is appearing in the game, so we know Sega is targeting big names for it. Or maybe it's the eagerly awaited Alien Isolation 2, although again, all of these games are already known about.
Meanwhile, the third season of Daredevil: Born Again approaches in 2027, which will reportedly end the Daredevil series. But: more Cox in video games - that has to be a good thing, right?

item.title: Ace Combat 8 has become the fastest-selling game in the aerial combat series, soaring to 1 million sales since its release roughly a week ago. Read more
item.description:
Ace Combat 8 has become the fastest-selling game in the aerial combat series, soaring to 1 million sales since its release roughly a week ago.
Bandai Namco announced the news in a press release, highlighting that the eighth mainline Ace Combat game is also the second highest-rated one, with a Metacritic review aggregate of between 86-88 percent. Ace Combat 4 is the series leader with 89.
Incidentally, Eurogamer hasn't reviewed Ace Combat yet but we have an appraisal in the works; apologies, it's been a busy season.
Ace Combat was released 2nd October and quickly recorded solid player-numbers on Steam, suggesting a degree of success. But it hasn't all been plane sailing - arf! - for Bandai Namco, with controversy surrounding the pack-in Ace Combat game The Belkan War, which wasn't standalone on PC as it was on console, causing various related issues.
One of the big additions in this iteration of Ace Combat 8 is a full suite of live service-like online multiplayer modes, which include co-op PvE modes, PvPvE modes, and a hub area where players can meet up and chat and parade around. Have you had a chance to play it yet?

item.title: The most touching of additions, in EA Sports FC 27, is a mode called The Grounds. This is an online social hub, where your custom avatar can roam and rise. It's touching not for its play – which lets you challenge people to rounds of Rush football, where the ghosts of Volta and Fifa Street happily haunt – but for its look. There are three open hub areas to explore, one styled on the UK, another on Paris, and a third on Argentina. The streets are clean, and cluttered by bustling NPCs. Here and there are luminous white-domed kiosks, with all the promise of an artist's impression of an upcoming Heathrow terminal. If I didn't know better, I'd say that the developers at EA Vancouver and EA Romania were paying homage to PlayStation Home. There, too, you could list through weird streets and glassy booths, clad in store-bought clothes, and beat other players in mini-games of all kinds. There, too, you felt the looming threat of a shutdown. Read more
item.description:
The most touching of additions, in EA Sports FC 27, is a mode called The Grounds. This is an online social hub, where your custom avatar can roam and rise. It's touching not for its play – which lets you challenge people to rounds of Rush football, where the ghosts of Volta and Fifa Street happily haunt – but for its look. There are three open hub areas to explore, one styled on the UK, another on Paris, and a third on Argentina. The streets are clean, and cluttered by bustling NPCs. Here and there are luminous white-domed kiosks, with all the promise of an artist's impression of an upcoming Heathrow terminal. If I didn't know better, I'd say that the developers at EA Vancouver and EA Romania were paying homage to PlayStation Home. There, too, you could list through weird streets and glassy booths, clad in store-bought clothes, and beat other players in mini-games of all kinds. There, too, you felt the looming threat of a shutdown.
Whether The Grounds will last I'm not sure. There is fleeting fun to be had. Rush is five-a-side, but you can also do one-on-one, two-on-two, and three-on-three modes. (The queuing is zippy, but you are occasionally undone by lag.) Plus, there are also goofy distractions, such as Balloon Ball, Bocce Ball, and Bucket Ball. These are spins on other games, the latter a basketball twist that has you dink high and dippy shots into a hoop. Frankly these diversions don't offer much nourishment. If EA really wanted to give staying power to The Grounds, a swift partnership with Sega would do the trick; imagine booting AiAi and his pals to and fro in frenzied rounds of Monkey Target. For more sober fare, there are also Clubhouse Matches, with full eleven-a-side games – though you can more quickly play others online in traditional exhibitions.
As it stands, The Grounds are shaky, but the good news this year is that the meat of the on-pitch action has been tuned up and slowed down. Here, of course, is where you might reasonably protest that the tuning-up and slowing-down is always the case. And that it's not just EA (over the course of several after-launch patches) but us who speed it back up again – who probe its gaps and find ways to bend the annual innovations toward exploitative silliness. In FC 25, for instance, the close-control dribble gave you the ability to rend chasms in an opposing team's press, and there are signs that FC 27 may yet suffer from an equivalent, in the off-balance dribble. This nifty quirk grants certain attackers the power of the Weeble: namely, to wobble and not fall down in the face of opposing pressure. They slip through a defender's rough jostle and stagger onwards. It looks great, and stressfully animated, which I imagine is exactly what you will be, after suffering it thirty or so times.
To step back a little, at the outset, in FC 27, you choose between Competitive Gameplay, which "favours speed, responsiveness, and reliable outcomes"; or Authentic Gameplay, "a new, slower-paced, more measured experience." I went for Authentic and am pleased to report that matches have a weightier texture. There is a greater emphasis on manual defending, with far less help from AI teammates. The Teammate Contain function now means that your AI defenders will mark an attacking player but keep a greater distance from them. This gives you more time to switch to right defender and take on the task manually. Switching to your desired defender is intuitive, and it feels good to snuff out an attack with clever positioning. Through balls – once the easy steak knife for the gristle of the back line – are harder to pull off, with lobbed versions currently in favour online. Matches play out in the midfield with pleasing heft, and the act of scoring a goal – the white ripple, the hum and shake of the stadium – is crunchy and thrilling.
Elsewhere, EA has rejigged set pieces, with corner kicks now slower and more cerebral. After the kick is taken, the camera zooms into the box; you can then make runs or shield the ball. The biggest change this year is Avoidance. Holding a shoulder button, you make your chosen player more slippy; like Altaïr in Assassin's Creed, they nudge and shimmy through crowds. It's a lively addition and adds a tactical edge. Crossing is now looser, with a ball more likely to find its way into a general area. This means you need to measure them out more, aim accurately, and develop a sense for pace and space.
Another of EA's proper-noun updates is Attacking Spatial Awareness. This, supposedly, makes your attacking teammates more likely to make intelligent runs – not, say, into crowded pockets but more propitious lanes of offence. Personally, I found this hit and miss. Maybe I lack the offensive nose to sniff out chances, but often I would pinball passes around the mid-field, only for one of my players to make a curving run away from the action before I clocked what they were up to. Still, if the takeaway from this is that Bruno Fernandes may just have a keener sense than I do about where I ought to pass, I'm happy to defer to him – and to apologise for my shortcomings if he feels sore about it.
What's more, teams are authentic to their real-life counterparts. With the various heartbreaks of summer still in mind, I first fired up an exhibition between Spain and Argentina. Sure enough, after a brace of yellows, a pulled shirt, and a hard shove, the result felt akin to the company of the Bolshoi Ballet squaring off against the cast of Rockstar's The Warriors. Less convincing are the swoops and flashes of the presentation. A meeting between Middlesbrough and Newcastle began with a satellite shot of the Earth, diving in cyber-zoom to the grounds of St. James' Park, as if it were the site of the next assignment for Captain Price and the merry men of Task Force 141.
Indeed EA Sports FC and Call of Duty share an odd resemblance. Both are the products of vast publishers. Both grind and shunt their way to a yearly schedule. Both, bewilderingly, have featured the likenesses of Lionel Messi, Neymar Jr., and Paul Pogba. And both yield a core experience wrapped in other modes that have, over time, become the bloated main event. For Activision, the single-player campaign increasingly seems weary and wan next to the behemoth of Warzone. For EA, the fundamental exhibition match, along with the Career mode, have given way to Ultimate Team.
FUT remains as morally murky and spirit-sapping as ever. The debate as to whether or not it constitutes gambling has been aired, and various countries have arrived at different conclusions. The technical answer, according to the UK Gambling Commission, is that, no, as the virtual items lack a mechanism to be cashed out for real currency, it isn't gambling. (In an interesting development, PEGI has certified the game a 16+, the first such certificate in the series, for its use of loot boxes.) But you can see why Victor Zagury, a Parisian lawyer who challenged EA in court, said to L'Équipe, about people hooked on Ultimate Team: "It is the logic of a casino that has entered their homes."
In FC 27, Ultimate Team is largely unchanged. You buy packs of random cards, with either earned FC Coins or real money, assemble squads, complete objectives, and battle other players online. The two most notable changes this year are the Gallery, and the way that squad-building challenges work. The Gallery has you array your cards as you would in a sticker book and earn Gallery Tokens, to be spent on kits and badges. As players and items pass through your Ultimate Team club, they can be enshrined in your Gallery. It's one part memory catalogue to one part deck builder. You can curate your Gallery into sets – clubs, nations, etc. – and these are then graded. You earn Gallery Tokens, which you can spend in the store on trinkets and cosmetics. Designed to deepen the essential draw of Ultimate Team, the Gallery feels surplus to requirements.
The more meaningful change is the way that squad-building challenges work. SBCs have been part of Ultimate Team for years, but in FC 27 they are faster. Rather than having to concentrate on your squad's chemistry or its overall rating, you can just submit items simply based on their rarity and ratings. It uses the same grade-scoring system that you have in the Gallery. Essentially, it means you can make partial progress faster, as you don't need to worry about the full requirements of every challenge. It's a smart tweak; it means quicker gratification and offers a more regular drip of reward. For those whose love the mode, Ultimate Team remains as moreish, frustrating, and brain-crackling as nicotine.
For those who prefer to stay away – and perhaps to sidestep the fuming ethical rumpus altogether – the Manager and Player Career modes have some welcome tweaks. Dynamic OVR, one of this year's better tweaks, has players' overall ratings fluctuate over the season. They have strong baseline abilities, of course; Dani Olmo is never going to plummet to a level where he would be happier in a Sunday League, but his form will surge and slump as matches wear on. It's a welcome change, giving a freer and more organic feel as the season passes. Injuries, play time, team-mate rivalries: there are a number of things that cause a player's Dynamic OVR to shift. It means your squad can punch above its own weight, if several of your players are performing above their usual form. It also means your success can be hampered, and that you need to make strategic changes.
Transfers are now slower, as you need to check with other clubs to see if any are actually possible, then negotiate a price, be it monetary, player swaps, or bonuses. Meanwhile, other clubs can swoop in and foment a bidding war. You will be relieved to hear that negotiations now take place in a dedicated and zippy menu. These are clean and intuitive, and see deals play out with a tension meter: high tension means that talks may break down, low tension that they are more likely to progress smoothly. You can negotiate with players directly and with clubs, and you can now opt to pay in installments – very useful if your budget is tight but you need an injection of star power.
There are also signing fees and agent fees to complicate proceedings. You can low-ball a club with your offer but sweeten the pot with a cluttering of bonuses. An extra five million if you qualify for the Champions League. Another couple million if they make over ten appearances, and so forth. There is a peculiar pleasure in sifting through these variables, in cleaning up a club's finances through shrewd business – or by being a bastard. Try slicing down an agent's fee or a weekly wage, leveraging a player's desire to be at your club (or their apathy toward another club trying to outbid you), despite raising tensions, and you feel Gordon Gekko on the beach with one of those mobile phones the size of a shoe. Throughout all this, there are also moments of randomness that make you laugh, such as an e-mail informing you that your centre forward has injured his hand in a cooking mishap, at home. So now you know: the threats that await any budding team include not just the whims of opposing managers and the perils of club debt, but an all-too-foolhardy attempt at risotto.
EA has made some solid iterations this year, then. The Grounds comes across as a frippery, Ultimate Team rumbles ever on, but FC 27 brings meaningful changes to the fluidity and speed of play. Given that its practical football-game monopoly is more or less unchallenged, EA could do a lot less than this (hardly the quote its PR people would want on the posters, granted), and in previous years it has done a lot less than this. But until something really moves underfoot, and someone else – FIFA and 2K seem likely – puts out a rival, this is what we have. An excellent on-pitch experience, packaged with cynicism, smart moves, controversy, and bursts of joy. Rather like football.
A copy of EA Sports FC 27 was provided for this review by EA Sports.

item.title: UPDATE 12PM BST: CD Projekt Red seems to have confirmed the partnership and film, with joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski commenting on X that: "We're excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise. We look forward to sharing more details at the appropriate time." Read more
item.description:
ORIGINAL STORY 11:40AM BST: A live-action Cyberpunk 2077 film is reportedly in the works at Paramount Pictures. Producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura - a former Warner Bros. exec influential in signing the The Matrix and Harry Potter films, and known for producing the Transformers films - is said to be attached to the project, with CD Projekt Red collaborating.
The report comes from Deadline, though the publication had no further information to share than what's above. CD Projekt Red told us it doens't have anything to share beyond what Nowakowski said on X.
Believing that CD Projekt Red would venture into live-action film territory doesn't take a stretch of the imagination. The company's Netflix anime partnership on Cyberpunk Edgerunners has been a success, with a second series due to air this month, on 20th October. The first season, released in 2022, was "fantastic", Wes wrote in his Cyberpunk Edgerunners impressions article, and amassed considerable Netflix viewing figures.
Live-action adaptations of video game-based series are also becoming increasingly popular, with The Last of Us and Fallout particularly finding wide success. CD Projekt Red being involved with the Cyberpunk 2077 adaptation would also somewhat heal a wound left by not being involved with The Witcher Netflix adaptation. CD Projekt art director Pawel Mileniczuk called this a "missed opportunity" when I talked to him for a Witcher 3 10-year anniversary article last year.
Meanwhile, CD Projekt Red is working on Cyberpunk 2, a project that's in pre-production, but with an expanding team - close to 200 people as of 31st July 2026 - full production doesn't seem far away. The sequel apparently adds a second city alongside the iconic Night City setting, and it's described as being like "Chicago gone wrong".
Should the live-action film prove real, and be made, the questions are what story will it tell - the same as in Cyberpunk 2077? - and which actors will play the game's well-known roles? The most famous of those roles is Keanu Reeves' portrayal of Johnny Silverhand, a character who used Reeves' likeness in the game. Could Reeves star in a film adaptation?
Cyberpunk 2077 was released in 2021, and its rocky launch has since become infamous. But CD Projekt Red did extensive work improving the game after release, focusing its efforts around a kind of 2.0 relaunch alongside the game's "remarkable" Phantom Liberty expansion, in 2023.
Paramount, meanwhile, recently acquired Warner Bros., and has since reorganised into mega-company Skydance. Activision's former leader Bobby Kotick has been employed on the board of it.

item.title: At today's Triple-i Showcase, Dave the Diver studio Mintrocket announced a surprisingly obvious, and perfectly fitting, collaboration. The game's final DLC, set for release in early 2027, brings the worlds of Subnautica 2 and Dave the Diver together. Read more
item.description:
At today's Triple-i Showcase, Dave the Diver studio Mintrocket announced a surprisingly obvious, and perfectly fitting, collaboration. The game's final DLC, set for release in early 2027, brings the worlds of Subnautica 2 and Dave the Diver together.
Although the two games share deep-sea exploration as a mechanic, they're at opposite ends of the spectrum tonally - though they're still a better fit than many of the other brands Dave the Diver has crossed over with. These have included Balatro, Yakuza, Godzilla, and Guilty Gear to name a few.
The upcoming Subnautica 2 DLC is free and was developed in collaboration with Subnautica 2 team Unknown Worlds. It brings Subnautica 2's ocean moon of Proteus to Dave the Diver, and sees Dave and Bancho - having discovered all species of sea creatures and associated sushi recipes in this dimension - travel to a new dimension to uncover more.
While there, yes, they're going to run into Subnautica 2's iconic Leviathan, but also make new friends and hopefully return home having made a lot of new discoveries. Jaeho Hwang, Mintrocket studio director said: "Both games are set underwater, but Subnautica has such a distinct approach to underwater exploration, so working with the Subnautica 2 team gave us a chance to bring a new wave to Dave the Diver experience."
Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos added: "It’s clear that we both adore one another’s games a lot, and the expansion is a love letter to both Dave the Diver and the Subnautica universe. People are in for a treat."
The Subnautica 2 x Dave the Diver crossover DLC is available to wishlist on Steam now. Subnautica 2, which launched in early access this year, has been incredibly successful. It sold more than 5 million copies in under a month, convincing publisher Krafton - which was embroiled in a legal battle with studio founders before launch - to turn it into a "franchise IP".

item.title: Former Activision boss Bobby Kotick has returned to a position of high influence as a board member of Skydance, the new entertainment juggernaut formed by the merging of Warner Bros. into Paramount. Read more
item.description:
Former Activision boss Bobby Kotick has returned to a position of high influence as a board member of Skydance, the new entertainment juggernaut formed by the merging of Warner Bros. into Paramount.
Kotick, who stepped down as Activision CEO following Xbox's $68.7bn acquisition of the company back in 2023, is joining the 13-person board alongside a selection of other newcomers. These include former UK prime minister Tony Blair, who is joining in an advisor role, and philanthropist Laurene Powell.
David Ellison, architect of the Warner Bros / Paramount merger, and Skydance's newly crowned CEO, issued the following statement: "I am delighted to welcome Laurene and Bobby to our Board and honored to have Tony join us as an Advisor. Bobby led a global entertainment company through three decades of sustained growth, and he brings real perspective on building enduring franchises and connecting with fans.
"His record of pairing bold strategic moves with disciplined capital allocation is exactly the experience we need as we bring our businesses together. Tony has led at the highest levels of government, respected for his intellect, strategic vision and ability to bring people together around bold, forward-looking ideas. His global perspective and insight will be invaluable as we turn ambition into results."
This merger has also resulted in the video game arms of both Warner Bros and Paramount being combined. Per Variety, the Skydance gaming division is now led by Tony Driscoll, who previously launched Fortnite's creator economy and ecosystem initiative between 2021 and 2024. That conjoined games divisions will have a variety of franchises at its fingertips, including Mortal Kombat, Mission Impossible, Avatar: The Last Airbender, and Harry Potter through Hogwarts Legacy 2.
In an email sent to staff and seen by Variety, Skydance president Andy Gordon wrote: "We're investing in our future growth engines alongside our core ambitions in TV, Film and direct-to-consumer: Games, Experiences, Consumer Products, and Publishing. These are core pillars of our strategy to build engagement and fandom in both the physical and digital worlds. We want to meet consumers where they watch, play, and engage. At the same time, we see opportunities to build on DC Comics' storytelling and expand our e-commerce offerings to connect fans with the brands they love."
Warner Bros has a lengthy, albeit rocky, history with video game development. While it has overseen some popular releases including Hogwarts Legacy and numerous Mortal Kombat games, recent years have not been as fruitful. Warner Bros Montreal suffered layoffs earlier this year, and Suicide Squad: Kill the Justice League developer Rocksteady was ravaged by staffing cuts in recent years.
Paramount, on the other hand, has a much more fledgling video games division. Its latest game, Avatar Legends: The Fighting game, has proven a niche yet adored release to genre diehards. Aside from that, it is also working with Platinum Games on TMNT: The Last Ronin, though a release date has yet to be announced.
Bobby Kotick led Activision during a period when the state of California sued the company for what it alleged was a "frat boy" company culture which created a "breeding ground for harassment and discrimination against women". Later, a Wall Street Journal report alleged that "Kotick knew for years about sexual-misconduct allegations". Bobby Kotick continues to deny the claims made in this Wall Street Journal report.
The report itself claims Kotick "received a troubling email in July 2018", and that "A lawyer for a former employee at Sledgehammer Games, an Activision-owned studio, alleged in the email that her client had been raped in 2016 and 2017 by her male supervisor after she had been pressured to consume too much alcohol in the office and at work events."
The Wall Street Journal claims this employee "reported the incidents to Sledgehammer's human-resources department and other supervisors, but nothing happened, according to the email, which threatened a lawsuit against the company."
It also reports that within months of receiving this email "Activision reached an out-of-court settlement with the woman, who also had reported one of the incidents to the police," and that "Kotick didn't inform the company’s board of directors about the alleged rapes or the settlement," according to people with knowledge of the board.
Last month, People Make Games released its own report focusing on Kotick's legal team's response to this report in the years since it was published. The PMG report, authored by journalist Mikhail Klimentov, cites a source who told Klimentov they had "received a letter from a defamation firm representing Bobby Kotick." This source, themself a journalist, had previously covered the Wall Street Journal's investigation into Kotick. Kliemtov said "this defamation firm was demanding that my source change their story", and that the firm representing Kotick had claimed the Wall Street Journal investigation "had been 'disproven'."
Klimentov also reported this legal letter "referenced a handful of other websites and publications that had seemingly given into this defamation firm's demands: Striking language the firm didn't like, adding editor's notes that referred to the Journal's investigation as 'debunked', and in at least one case deleting an article entirely."
Despite these claims, however, the original Wall Street Journal report remains live and unchanged.

item.title: Riot Games has released a final gameplay trailer for 2XKO, its short-lived fighting game set to be sunsetted later this year. The game is going out with a bang, with a shock reveal of a secret character coming alongside the games last major update. Read more
item.description:
Riot Games has released a final gameplay trailer for 2XKO, its short-lived fighting game set to be sunsetted later this year. The game is going out with a bang, with a shock reveal of a secret character coming alongside the games last major update.
This final major update, set to go live on the 27th October, was previously confirmed to feature Samira as the game's 16th character. This trailer features a showcase of her move set in action, however she shares the spotlight with Sett, a character who had been long requested from fans.
Sett, a bulky brawler, is seen to possess a combination of shattering blows and powerful grabs in this trailer. A significant difference between his 2XKO abilities and the kit available to him in League of Legends is a powered-up state which appears to intensify many of his special moves, granting them new and dangerous properties. One of his supers also appears to show him grabbing both characters on the enemy team at once, slamming them together in a homage to his MOBA manifestation.
2XKO was in development at Riot Games for a long time, and released earlier this year to much fanfare from fighting game fans. Unfortunately, the development team responsible for it almost immediately suffered layoffs, and later the 2XKO's end of service was announced as player retention was not strong enough to justify the cost of support of additional work on the game beyond its first season of character releases.
Nonetheless, it is a game with a lot of merit. It's also not vanishing forever unlike other live service games who have followed a similar path. The game will remain playable for the foreseeable future, and the microtransaction store has been taken out and replaced with an optional one-time purchase that unlocks the full suite of in-game cosmetics, save perhaps for a Chipotle promotional avatar outfit. As such, those excited by Sett's reveal can enjoy messing around with him later this month.

item.title: GTA 6 will let you listen to radio stations while not in a car, by wearing headphones and earbuds connected to smartphones. GTA 6 also introduces on-demand podcasts, so you can binge true crime while also doing true crime - something like that. Read more
item.description:
GTA 6 will let you listen to radio stations while not in a car, by wearing headphones and earbuds connected to smartphones. GTA 6 also introduces on-demand podcasts, so you can binge true crime while also doing true crime - something like that.
"For the first time ever, Grand Theft Auto 6 introduces a series of on-demand podcasts for Jason and Lucia to experience beyond Leonida's terrestrial radio," Rockstar wrote on its website, "with both radio and podcasts available to listen to in vehicles and on foot through newly introduced headphones and earbuds connected to their smartphones."
Rockstar announced these additions while detailing six of radio stations coming to GTA 6, which appear to be hosted by incredibly famous real-world singers (according to Rolling Stone), while offering musical previews of what we'll hear there.
It's an incredibly expensive line-up for a game that has been made with no expense spared. As Christian Donlan noted after watching Netflix's extended GTA 6 reveal: this is what a billion dollars gets you.
The timing of this GTA 6 announcement coincides with another huge GTA 6 gameplay footage leak by CyberLeek, which shows nudity, dirt-biking and a developer menu. CyberLeek activity had seemed to have stopped following Rockstar parent company Take-Two taking legal action to track them down and find them, but this latest development suggests they're still at large.
Meanwhile, GTA 6 edges ever closer to its 19th November release, while Rockstar Games also fights an employment tribunal case in Scotland linked to alleged union busting.

item.title: CD Projekt Red has rolled out a substantial patch for the new Witcher 3 Remastered edition of the game, notably adding more lighting-related options to the console versions of the game, such as Bloom, enabling you to turn them off, should you wish. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has rolled out a substantial patch for the new Witcher 3 Remastered edition of the game, notably adding more lighting-related options to the console versions of the game, such as Bloom, enabling you to turn them off, should you wish.
CD Projekt Red also noted it was working on an update for the Switch 2 version of The Witcher 3 Remastered to get "closer parity between all versions of the game", and to improve image "clarity and sharpness". More information on the Switch 2 patch is coming in the "following days".
Notable fixes in Witcher 3 patch 5.01 - out now on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X - include fixes to dodging and odd bugs such as those where Geralt's stamina would suddenly deplete when sprinting and dodging at the same time. Player-controlled boats shouldn't "start moving uncontrollably" any more, which is a relief, ladder "interactions" have been improved, and witcher mentor Vesemir won't keep repeating himself when you cast the Quen Sign.
PC fixes address faults like incorrect graphics settings being applied - and in some circumstances the wrong GPU being selected for use, bizarrely - whereas console changes introduce promised performance improvements as well as voiceover volume improvements, and fixes for incorrect frame-rate limits being applied.

The Witcher 3 Remastered edition arrived for free early last week, representing an extraordinarily generous update which refreshes and revitalises the beloved RPG game. Millions of players flocked back to The Witcher 3 to play it, but not all received the update well, mostly because of bugs introduced, but also because of visual changes some felt overly brightened the game. Hence CD Projekt Red's busy patching work.
All of this work on The Witcher 3 is being done ahead of the game's unprecedented third expansion Songs of the Past arriving next year - unprecedented because I can't recall another single-playing RPG having an expansion 12 years after it was released. Songs of the Past adds a whole new countryside region to the game called Letten to explore, and an adventure themed around Dandelion and his family to follow. Dom saw Songs of the Past in action at Gamescom recently and came away impressed. "Songs of the Past has been a great reminder: CDPR's writing is some of gaming's very best," Dom wrote.

item.title: We're big fans of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, having given the fast and punishing racing game five stars in our review. We also spoke to developer Fuse Games to better understand how it recaptured the Burnout spirit so well in the game. And it was then we heard about Fuse's unique approach to prototyping Galactic Racer. Read more
item.description:
We're big fans of Star Wars: Galactic Racer, having given the fast and punishing racing game five stars in our review. We also spoke to developer Fuse Games to better understand how it recaptured the Burnout spirit so well in the game. And it was then we heard about Fuse's unique approach to prototyping Galactic Racer.
"What's the fastest way we can get ideas down and then talk about them?" Fuse Games CEO Matt Webster told Eurogamer. "Modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of it in-software, but there's still something [about that which is] not as fast as getting a written idea down."
Creative director Kieran Crimmin added: "There's a prototyping tool for every kind of system that you want to prototype, and the one that you pick should be the one that gets you there the quickest, and gets you to validate the emotion the quickest."
In Galactic Racers' case, the tool was a board game, which had Post-It notes stuck to it that the team used to map out the game's upgrades and meta progression systems. "I mean, I say 'board game': a lot of it is Post-Its and a scribble and some dice," Crimmins said. "But we're trying to validate those feelings as quickly as possible, o you just pick the best tool for the moment."
Elsewhere in the interview, Crimmins explained the importance of distilling game-feel in playable game prototypes and testing them quickly to see if players shared the same feelings about them.
"We like many things," Crimmins said. "We have loads of ideas, and we have references and emotions that we're trying to get to. But you can't know if you've got game-feel. You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system. So we just try and get into [the] prototype [stage], get it into our players' hands. See if they're feeling those emotions.
"Rather than worry about whether it's the right set of things," Crimmins added, "we worry about getting it as a play experience as quickly as possible and seeing if it feels right."
In the Star Wars: Galactic Racer Eurogamer review, Christian Donlan was enamoured with the game's ability to merge modern games' unlockables and Roguelite traits with the tight course design of classic games. "Galactic Racer never forgets that between the loot and the loadout and the story choices this is still a racing game. The game has that ceaseless full-ahead pelt that Burnout offers and each corner is a set-piece, even before you tip your Skim Speeder onto one edge," Donlan wrote.

item.title: The week of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ reveals continues, and the latest highlighted a questionable addition that seems to offer an unfair advantage in an extraction shooter. Read more
item.description:
The week of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ reveals continues, and the latest highlighted a questionable addition that seems to offer an unfair advantage in an extraction shooter.
The DMZ progression trailer, which went live overnight, is mainly centered around the out-of-match metagame. Between rounds, players can spend time at the Forward Operating Base (FOB) to upgrade and customise weapons, unlock new skills for their operators, create useful items using the 3D printer, and prepare for their next deployment. Much of this was revealed earlier in the week.
But one new thing that stood out was how players will load into the match - and what they can load in with. As seen in the video, there are five ways for players to 'infil' into a match, varied by cost. These range from being free to costing a whopping $100,000 in DMZ Cash per deployment.
The free option spawns your character on foot at a random point, which has long been the default option in all other extraction shooters, as it ensures players start each match equally. But Modern Warfare 4 DMZ takes that several steps further.
The next infil option costs $5,000 and spawns the squad in a Polaris Dagor A1, a tactical off-road vehicle, offering a significant speed advantage. If you're willing to spend $25,000 to deploy, meanwhile, you'll do so in a Light Tactical Vehicle (LTV), which has considerably more armour. The Call of Duty Blog says the version found across DMZ's map has an optional .50 Cal turret, but it's not clear whether the LTV you can spawn in has one.
Then there's the $50,000 option, which spawns the squad in a helicopter, which represents an enormous advantage over people spawning on foot. But by far the most ludicrous option is the $100,000 tier, an air vehicle, which looks like the cargo plane you jump out of at the start of battle royale matches in games like Warzone. This, presumably, allows the squad to pick the specific point on the map they want to start at - a luxury other players won't have as spawn points in DMZ are randomised.
Now, it's worth pointing out that unlocking the ability to spawn in the LTV and helicopter is locked behind completing a separate story mission for each option, meaning they won't immediately be available to players even if they can afford it.
That said, all of the non on-foot options offer clear advantages. A player in a buggy can zoom around the map quickly, clearing objectives one after another. A squad in a helicopter can do that even faster, potentially flying directly to a boss' spawn location to kill it and extract early. And as those vehicles persist throughout the match, it's possible - assuming they're not destroyed or abandoned - for a squad to efficiently jump between points of interest before heading to the extraction point, making for a far less risky deployment.
Incidentally, Reality, one of Call of Duty's longtime leakers, revealed these options last year, alongside DMZ's different weather conditions. In their post on X, they said the last paid spawn option - the aircraft - is an AC-130 gunship, the devastating multiplayer Killstreak with multiple heavy guns mounted on it. The AC-130 is often confused with its cargo and transport sibling the C-130, which is probably what's happened here, because starting the match with such a high-power attack vehicle would ruin the experience for all other players.
I can imagine weeks or months into DMZ's life, as players' cash reserves grow and they become more familiar with the map and where everything is, free spawns will turn into the poor, new player option, inevitably putting them at an immediate disadvantage.
How Infinity Ward balances all that remains to be seen, but seeing the confusion about the existence of a PvE-only mode within DMZ doesn't fill me with a lot of hope. DMZ launches with Modern Warfare 4 on 23rd October for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.description:
Today, Microsoft announced it is setting up a new branch of the Xbox business named XP. In a blog over at the Xbox Wire, Microsoft details what this new area of the business looks like - it consists of four branches: Xbox Places, Xbox Pictures, Xbox Partnerships, Xbox Products.
"[XP] brings together capabilities that have existed across various teams at Xbox for years and aligns them behind a shared mission: helping our franchises reach more people, create deeper connections with players and new fans, and unlock new opportunities for these fandoms to grow around the world," says a press release from Matthew Ball, chief strategy officer at Xbox. "Great games remain at the center of these franchises and at the heart of Xbox. XP will partner with the best creative minds across our studios, along with trusted partners, to build on that foundation and create more ways for people to experience the worlds they love."
A large focus of Microsoft's newest investment will be in cross-media partnerships, looking particularly at film and TV. It seems lots of publishers are eyeing up the film industry, no doubt buoyed by the massive success of titles like the Super Mario Bros. and Super Mario Galaxy movies (which have earned $1.36bn and $1bn, respectively) and Sony's recently released Resident Evil movie (which is tracking at $280m+ at the time of writing). Xbox has had its own notable successes on the big screen, too: last year A Minecraft Movie amassed more than $550m (£415m) in two weeks, immediately setting up a sequel.
Xbox has also experimented with TV in the past, too. Fallout is the highlight for the company at the moment, with Fallout Season 2 boasting 83 million viewers tuning in during its first 13 weeks of release. Less successful was Paramount's divisive Halo TV show, which was cancelled after two seasons. A question that springs to my mind when reading this is: where will we go next? There are plenty of Xbox franchises that'd make for good TV; Perfect Dark, Fable, and maybe even a Forza story in the style of Sony's peculiar Gran Turismo show would work. I know the initial run at a Halo TV show was a bit of a flop, but I'd love to see a limited series on the Fall of Reach. It'd make some fine prestige television. We know there's a Gears of War film and a Sea of Thieves film in production, too.
Elsewhere, there's Xbox Places. This is the arm of the company that'll oversee the Minecraft theme parks that are opening in the US and UK that so far represent over £85m of investment from Mojang and Xbox. They're expected to open 'between 2026 and 2027'. Will we hear about more real-life locations that'll fall under the 'Places' banner? It remains to be seen.
All these initiatives will no doubt require staffing, which is such to be a sore subject for any of the staff that have been impacted by wide-ranging cuts at Microsoft and Xbox over the past few years. Given the contraction of its game studios and software business, is Xbox trying to recoup costs by pursuing other avenues for growth? It certainly seems like it.

item.description:
How do you revive a series like Hellraiser? When your source material spans four decades and multiple mediums, all with wildly differing tones (and fans), what stays, what goes? Where would you even begin? It's a question developer Saber Interactive seems to struggle with throughout Hellraiser: Revival and the result is a messy, uneven, but earnest, and often fascinating sort of tribute that, boldly, goes back to the start.
Clive Barker's 1986 novella The Hellbound Heart, the genesis of the Hellraiser series, is a queer horror classic; a story of obsession and addiction, loosely inspired by the gay BDSM scene. Later Hellraiser movies would see the series devolve into silliness, iconic villain Pinhead (played by Doug Bradley, who briefly returns here) becoming a quipping counterpart to the Freddies and Chuckies of the time. But Saber seems to have more literary ambitions, drawing heavily on Barker's original themes for its tale of two lovers and their encounter with the Cenonbites; extradimensional beings from a realm where agony and ecstasy are interwined.
It's a story that starts with sweaty softcore sex and soon descends into flesh-ripping violence, setting protagonist Aiden against a quasi-religious, extreme BDSM cult as he desperately attempts to rescue his girlfriend Sunny back from Hell. Unfortunately, their relationship is so immediately toxic, it's hard to get emotionally invested in this critical narrative throughline.
Tonally, Hellraiser is a strange game. Instead of artfully orchestrated scares, Revival's horrors rely on a grim procession of fused and rended flesh, as relentless as it is effectively offputting. But the ceaseless bodily destruction sits awkwardly alongside villains so deliriously flamboyant, they'd be twiddling their moustaches if it weren't for their masks. And attempts at eroticism and sensuality quickly short circuit amid the dildo-strewn nightclub neon, where extras spit out porn-calibre line readings of flat innuendo. Narratively, it's also a bit of a mess; too obvious and too incoherent by turns, clumsily walking through a minefield of complex ideas - most obviously, the intersection of sex and violence - with all the subtly and nuance of a double-A FPS with an interactive paddle spanking scene. But to its credit, it just about manages to avoid feeling exploitative, and there is, I think, an earnestness to Revival that carries it through.
This is the work of a studio, you sense, with a genuine love of the source material - and a desire to do it justice too. And that manifests in a game willing to take some unexpectedly big swings. They don't always work, but at least it's interesting. Take combat, for instance. Revival is, foundationally at least, a fairly bog standard FPS, and it's not long before an early dalliance with perfunctory stealth makes way for more confrontational action. You start with a pistol and, slowly, your arsenal swells to include a shotgun, a revolver, an SMG, and more; an enigmatic old woman intermittently setting up stall to sell you new toys and upgrades (it's not the only time Revival feels like it's channeling Resident Evil 4). Eventually, you're mowing down the Unworthy armed with laser-sight pointers and incendiary shells, which should be the absolute antithesis of horror, but Saber just about makes it work.
For starters, Aiden moves with a satisfying sense of physicality. He wobbles when he runs, sidesteps with weighty momentum, and, when the melee weapons come out, he bludgeons and slices with sickeningly tangible abandon. And while Revival is undoubtedly action-heavy, Saber still finds tension in withholding. Weapons break, ammo is short, and even the most basic enemies take a good few hits to bring down. Throw in armoured foes which need to be stripped first - either with a swing of something heavy or a particularly aggressive blast - and every combat encounter feels like it's perpetually teetering on the brink of disaster. But Revival strikes a good balance between stressful and unduly punishing.
And while I don't love the modern day proliferation of crafting systems, the focus on furious scavenging here feels additive. It heightens the sense of last-gasp desperation as you pocket anything and everything, in the hope you've got enough to eke out a couple more health packs or bullets when things go wrong. Your limited inventory space, meanwhile, forces some tough choices as you frantically shuffle, stash, or abandon items, optimistically Tetrising together the most effective arsenal from the scraps at your disposal.
Later, Hellraiser's iconic puzzle box - here, the Genesis Configuration - essentially becomes a gravity gun, so you can fling sawblades, spikes, even fireballs, shredding through multiple bodies as one. And if you're short on the Suffering needed to power it, near-dead enemies wobble on their last legs so you can gruesomely syphon it out of them. Combat's pilfered parts might feel Resident Evil by way of Half-Life and Doom, but at its best, Hellraiser finds an enjoyably ad hoc rhythm of its own - creating showdowns of pure frantic panic as you scramble to juggle weapons that seem to empty their ammo in seconds, as you furiously scan your surroundings for something pointy to use as a projectile, and delve into your inventory, desperately jettisoning stuff to make space for whatever feels most pressing right now.
The trouble is Revival spends a lot of time failing to make the most of its tools. Particularly in the first half of the game, progress feels like a linear sequence of encounters that are over before they've even begun, so quick to wrap up there's no space to settle into anything like a rewarding combat rhythm. (Conversely, bosses tend to drag on a touch too long.) And it tends to make for a lot of uninspiring busywork in a game that's already erratically paced, often adopting the relaxed meandering of a walking sim. And while I get what Saber is going for with its inventory system, constantly having to pause a big fight to manually switch weapons in and out of the limited equip-slots feels like a faff too far, and kills momentum.
What saves it though are the set-pieces: cabin in the woods ambushes where you're suddenly expected to furiously board up the windows while the Unworthy pour in; locked-room face-offs against grasping horrors that can melt into the floor while you've barely space to turn, and swerves into smoky hide-and-seek creeping. There's rarely a big encounter that doesn't throw in a new twist, and it lends Revival an infectious unpredictability that permeates everything.
Few of Hellraiser: Revival's ideas are original, admittedly (it even nicks Skyrim's lockpick mini-game), but it's hard to be bored in a game that pingpongs so incessantly. And just when its real-world action feels like it's starting to sag, proceedings are usually buoyed by Aiden's extra-dimensional jaunts into the Labyrinth, where the Cenobites and their demonic deity Leviathan reside. Revival is a good-looking game, but it's here - in Hellraiser's Escher-esque, non-Euclidean nightmare of endless, impossibly configured stone - that Saber's artistry really shines.
I am, I'll admit, a sucker for video games that delight in impossible spaces, so there's definitely some bias here. But the Labyrinth's confounding abstractions are a real high point; trading uneven combat for a shift into puzzles, platforming, and pursuit.
It's rarely complicated stuff: you'll dodge vicious blades and sneak around violently whirring traps; you'll stealth to avoid the watchful eye of Leviathan, or use your Genesis Configuration to shift monolithic blocks and create new paths. But when the blocks you're shifting are vast spirals of grinding stone, or staircases that seem to unfold on themselves, spinning around as gravity shifts on its axis, sending the world into a disorientating vortex of movement and sound, it massively elevates the whole thing. Likewise, there are a handful of arresting PT-inspired sequences, where memories melt into unreality under the Leviathan's gaze, and even some genuinely effective chase sequences as you flee from a relentless Chatterer - the Labyrinth endlessly reconfiguring itself around you in real-time. These are perhaps the standout moments; melding spectacle and tension without descending into frustration.
Hellraiser: Revival is not, I don't think, a great game. It's too messy and inconsistent to earn that accolade. And there are times - particularly in its uneven opening half - when I wouldn't even say it's a good game. Tonally and narratively, it's all over the place, stumbling where nuance is required and struggling to create a strong emotional throughline. It borrows so much for its gameplay grab-bag that it often struggles to find its own identity whenever the Cenobites and the Labyrinth are off-screen. Its action sometimes sags too. But slowly, it begins to find a more confident rhythm. Its combat and encounters grow more engaging, making the most of its tools. And as the line between the Labyrinth and the real-world blurs, the erratic tone settles and the best bits of both halves start to merge. Hellraiser: Revival might be scrappy and inconsistent, but it's entertaining, and even when it's not, it's at least fascinating. Which probably also describes the series as a whole. A bit of pleasure, a bit of pain - how apt!
A copy of Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival was provided for this review by Saber Interactive.

item.title: World of Warcraft: Forever's developers have announced drastic visual changes to the game's new Skyborne race following passionate community feedback. These include new in-game models that better represent the game's early MMO aesthetic, much to the community's delight. Read more
item.description:
World of Warcraft: Forever's developers have announced drastic visual changes to the game's new Skyborne race following passionate community feedback. These include new in-game models that better represent the game's early MMO aesthetic, much to the community's delight.
The World of Warcraft community first caught wind of these changes during a recent episode of the official World of Warcraft: Forever podcast, in which senior game designer Josh "Aggrend" Greenfield acknowledged impassioned feedback of the Skyborne humanoid and druid character models. While he didn't have anything to announce then, he said the team "hoped to have something more substantive to say pretty soon". And "pretty soon" now seems to have arrived.
The blog post detailing these changes, published on the World of Warcraft website, starts by establishing the team's aim to "uphold the original WoW era aesthetic" while offering more choice in how they experience Azeroth. It then admits that some of the team's ideas around the visual fidelity of certain new additions missed the mark: specifically the Skyborne models. The blog notes: "The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world."
Both versions of the Skyborne elves in World of Warcraft: Forever will be altered to better align with the rest of the game. The blog shows side-by-side comparison before-and-after images, which highlight the models' softness being removed, colour saturation lowered, and more detailed fur textures added.
Perhaps what's more exciting, especially to World of Warcraft: Forever players who value retro visuals, is word of planned changes to the standard definition models. The blog agrees with feedback that the standard definition Skyborne models could feel "jarring" next to the game's legacy races, and confirms that new standard definition models are in the works, with a planned release in early 2027. For now, an image of work-in-progress characters was included. Look at those sharp angles! You could cut an apple on those.
Shimmying over to the popular World of Warcraft Reddit, and the mood is similarly joyful. Notably, many players are expressing their appreciation at the WoW Forever team's eagerness to respond to community feedback so quickly and openly. One popular thread is titled: "Ignore the toxic positivity. Disregard the brigaders. Keep giving feedback. Keep being vocal. Forever team is GOATed and they're listening." The thread highlights not only these changes, but also the recent decision by Blizzard to lower the rarity of dungeon loot so quest rewards aren't devalued, and the decision to change the races' headshots in the character creator from Modern WoW's headshots to those found in Classic WoW.
"The fact that they tweaked these rather minor things and even changed the icons is honestly in my eyes monumental," wrote user Ubberman. "Who are these people? That is an exceedingly high response rate and for rather minor things that only add to the feel. If they keep this up for even a year, WoW Forever will genuinely be the best World of Warcraft version to date. Genuinely."
World of Warcraft: Forever may still only be in beta, but it's already proving mighty popular. The server cap had to be increased due to player demand, and early critique of this introductory version of the upcoming MMO - including ours - is largely positive. WoW Forever launches in full on 4th November.
