item.description:
Google and Unity yesterday announced new generative-AI game-making platforms designed to make and shape games by inputting text prompts. Google's product is called Playground and is available for testing now, if you live in the US, and Unity's product is Unity Spark and is "coming soon".
Their side-by-side announcements are more than coincidence. Google Playground will work with and integrate Unity Spark when "creators" want to "expand their concepts" with "robust, professional-level mechanics, high-fidelity 3D capabilities", Google's Playground blog post said.
Given that, there's a sort of two-tiered approach going on here. Google Playground is the entry level platform, a much more - excuse me while I throw-up on myself - 'vibe-coded' idea origination tool. It's the sort of thing you plug a load of words into the text box, presumably while marvelling at your own creativity and taking lifestyle selfies on a beach somewhere, while Google Playground builds a fairly simple game. Then, when you're happy with it, and AI-prompting a post on LinkedIn about your career change, you can share the game with other Playground users.
Said Google: "Games are one of the most creative forms of expression, and the gaming community keeps growing. But game creation has historically been limited to a select group of people who have technical experience and knowledge of complex game engines. Today, we're introducing Playground, an experimental gaming platform that lets you create, play, and share custom games. Playground lowers the barriers to creation, so bringing game ideas to life can now be as easy as describing it through a few prompts — no coding experience required."
Unity Spark, on the other hand, is a more complicated affair. There are text prompts but they work more as shortcuts or helpers within Unity's more traditional game engine package, so it's not just a 'whack a load of text in, sit back, and create' kind of affair. Indeed, in an interview with Gamefile, Unity boss Matt Bromberg underlined this point, stating that Spark was not about "one-shotting" game development.
"I'm not denigrating folks who are interested in one-shotting things," Bromberg said. "I think there's a level of excitement and enthusiasm about what the technology can do. And maybe that's just a way of people celebrating it." But, he said: "Unity Spark is not going to be for everyone. There are many people who don't have the patience and ambition to make something real.
"Asking the AI to reproduce a game that has already been made does not make you [Hideo] Kojima. It doesn't make you a famous game developer any more than typing the first paragraph of War and Peace into your word processor makes you Tolstoy."
One of the major features of Unity Spark is the ability to co-create games with other people in real-time, and a Unity Spark video showed this in action, with a pair of people - Mari and Theo - making their dream game, Space Corridor. It's a pretty rubbish sci-fi shooter, albeit one that's made quickly, and we see obvious complexity in the engine while it's being made.
Gamefile saw Unity Spark demonstrated live, and apparently it pulled assets from Unity's Store for use. Where Google Playground pulls art and assets from, we don't know - Google didn't say. Gamefile also quizzed Bromberg about the carbon footprint of Spark, which presumably requires a lot of power to build games. Could there be an estimated carbon footprint cost next to requests? "We hadn't considered that," Bromberg replied. "That's something worth considering."
Unity isn't the first game engine to heavily incorporate generative-AI, though. Epic Games revealed a big gen-AI push this summer for its ubiquitous game engine Unreal, incorporating large language model support into its current generation of Unreal, and targeting foundational integration of LLMs for Unreal Engine 6. Even Capcom is evolving its in-house RE Engine "for the AI generation", to incorporate help with coding, QA testing, and more.

item.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute delight to play, and for fans of the Burnout games, it can feel like coming home. That's hardly surprising given that Fuse Games, the creators of Galactic Racer, contains an awful lot of DNA from Burnout's old home at Criterion. Read more
item.description:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute delight to play, and for fans of the Burnout games, it can feel like coming home. That's hardly surprising given that Fuse Games, the creators of Galactic Racer, contains an awful lot of DNA from Burnout's old home at Criterion.
But what does it mean for a game to feel like Burnout? And how do you make a game that channels the junky, battered-tech side of Star Wars? I spoke to some of the people behind Galactic Racer to find out.
So here's a quick chat with Matt Webster, the CEO of Fuse Games, along with Kieran Crimmins, the creative director at Fuse, and Craig Derrick, executive producer at Lucasfilm Games. It touches on everything from "game feel" and emotion to board game prototypes and Richard Donner's Superman.
I had a moment when I started my first game, and I set off, and I waited until I would normally press boost in Burnout, and then I pressed the boost button from Burnout, and it did exactly what I thought it was going to do if I had been playing Burnout. I think a lot of people know your lineage from Criterion. They will be thinking along the same lines as I was, and I wondered how you feel about people having that experience: the rediscovery of the Burnout boost.
I think that what you're describing is not just the boost mechanic: press a button and go faster. It's everything that happens when you depress that button. We reduce it down into: button goes down, speed goes up. But there is clearly more going on there. But yeah, the game feel part is extraordinarily important. It's a throughline throughout the entire experience. Because if you can suspend your disbelief on a primary sensory level, then we can immerse you so much more powerfully in everything else that's going on as well.
Does this search for game feel help to dictate the way you approach Star Wars? This is the Star Wars of brilliant but sometimes decrepit technology that can go really fast but can also break at the worst moment.
Matt Webster: That's not us. That's this wonderful galaxy that we get to play in. It's all there for us to lean into. The game is a combination of our love of racing and our love of Star Wars. We come at it as fans, and we see those details too, and it's just that we have the wonderful privilege to be able to put some of them into action. The tactile nature: bashing something to get it to work. I always call that "touch sensitive", right? That leads to flicking levers and doing button combinations at race start. That's never getting old. That's the thing that connects you into the tactility of the galaxy.
When I look at Burnout, there's a grippiness to that game. In Paradise, you feel like your wheels are almost traveling in grooves in the road. So when you approach a game where you don't have wheels, how do you get a sense of connection to the road?
Matt Webster: What you're just describing again is an attention to game feel that I think we have a very particular point of view on. It just so happened in something like Burnout, for us at least, the best way around a corner in a car is sideways with all four wheels straight. But that's actually quite difficult to do. To deconstruct the intention there: the average driver doesn't think they're an average driver, right? We all think that we're incredible. And that's the fantasy we're trying to do here. The starting fantasy is to be an incredible racing pilot.
And actually it's pretty liberating to be decoupled from tyres on tarmac. We can do different things, exciting things. We can amplify the vertical. We can amplify the angles. But it's all built on some pretty significant foundations. Which are: if you could invent a levitating jet engine on Earth, it would behave in this way because we built a simulation to deliver it. And the reason you do that is because we've all got an innate understanding of the physical world around us. There is a physical simulation going on there. And it's inspired by everything that we've seen about Star Wars, from the podracers to the land speeders to the speeder bikes to every vehicle that we've seen there.
When you pay so much attention to game feel and you control the experience in that way to give players a very specific sensation, what's it like to then add Roguelite features and give players control over what they build? Does that feel like giving away control or does it feel like something else?
Matt Webster: Fundamentally we define the container. And because those rulesets and those systems are cared for and crafted and balanced. We want to push the genre forward. I [often] talk about [how] arcade is not the absence of depth. It's your route into it. And then we reveal that depth in accessible and approachable ways for you to go and play.
Kieran Crimmins: And the things you're [building your vehicle with], we would call our player story generator. The point of creating all these physical toys, which is essentially what they are from a fundamental level, is so that you can play with them like you would play with your toys. That means stacking them on top of each other, creating something that you wouldn't expect. But then it reacts in a way that feels physical and real and expected, but it's also yours. What we try to do is create moments of emotion for players. I mean, game design, on this fundamental level, is systems that create emotions, right? So we target emotions from Star Wars. We target emotions from racing. We target emotions from the story, and then we turn them into play. We turn them into interactive experiences. So we don't need to curate everything that happens along a timeline because we give you a set of toys that are the experiences that create that racing thrill.
Is it hard to put all those pieces together? The vehicle parts and upgrades?
Kieran Crimmins: We like many things. We have loads of ideas, and we have references and emotions that we're trying to get to. But you can't know if you've got game feel. You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system. So we just try and get into [the] prototype [stage], get it into our players' hands. See if they're feeling those emotions. So rather than worry about whether it's the right set of things, we worry about getting it as a play experience as quickly as possible and seeing if it feels right. And that's how we ended up with those things [we have to play with in the game]. They were actually part of the original board game for the early prototype.
I've got to stop you. Tell me about the board game prototype.
Matt Webster: It's a prototyping story. What's the fastest way we can get ideas down and then talk about them. You know, modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of in software, but there's still something [about that that is] not as fast as getting a written idea down. From a board game perspective, you sort of decouple yourself from a particular prototype and you're talking about moment–to–moment.
Kieran Crimmins: There's a prototyping tool for every kind of system that you want to prototype, and the one that you pick should be the one that gets you there the quickest, and gets you to validate the emotion the quickest. So when it came to upgrades and meta progression, I can do a board game in a day. I mean, I say "board game". A lot of it is Post–its and a scribble and some dice. But we're trying to validate those feelings as quickly as possible. So you just pick the best tool for the moment.
I'm struck by how much you talk about emotions in your game design process.
Craig Derrick: Emotions are the new verbs, you know. Kieran, you're going to nail this, but I'm just going to say, when we're talking about the experience of play and the agency that you want to feel through those moment–to–moment experiences, how can you not describe it as an emotional state?
Kieran Crimmins: I think you're absolutely right. I think it's fair to say, what's the point in all this if you're not feeling something? Yeah. Like whether that's games, walking through the park, whatever it is, that is the ultimate goal: to create some strong emotions, and that be some sort of reflection of your thing of playing. It's always been at the heart of everything we do everywhere I've worked where we make games.
Matt Webster: Maybe as an industry we don't talk about it enough, but when we talk about games, we're actually talking about how it made us feel. So it is always is all about emotion, whether it's the sensory feel or the or the emotional feel or the what's motivating me. I tell this story a lot. One of the original superhero movies was the original Superman, directed by Richard Donner. I remember watching the DVD extras, and he was sat in front of his production desk talking about the movie, and behind him was this massive word, and it said 'Verisimilitude." I had to look it up. It was graffitied on the wall behind him.
And essentially, it means the truth of the thing, or the truth of the heart. It stuck with me a lot, right? Because what he said was, "If you don't believe a man can fly, it doesn't matter what else we do. If, fundamentally, you don't believe a man can fly, nothing's going to work."
So if you don't believe that you are in the Star Wars galaxy, that you are piloting this land speeder around at 600 kilometers an hour. If you don't believe that, then it doesn't matter what story we're doing, the awesome stuff that we're doing in the paddock, and this sports story that we're telling. If you don't believe that at the heart, then we can't do all the other stuff. And that brings us back to that starting point of why that sort of stuff is really important, on that very base, foundational level.

item.description:
Last year, we learned that Xbox cancelled a reboot of Perfect Dark. The game, in development at The Initiative, was cancelled as part of 2025's wave of wide-ranging cuts at Microsoft and Xbox. In 2026, of course, things have only gotten worse for the company.
Over the past 24 hours, leaked gameplay footage of the Perfect Dark reboot has surfaced online, giving us a glimpse at what could have been. The gameplay, first unearthed by MP1ST, shows off a few of the different weapons protagonist Joanna Dark would have been able to use, as well as a few different environments she'd have been sneaking and fighting her way through. MP1ST claims the footage it uncovered - which has since spread around various social media accounts - comes from a VFX artist that "has previous experience working on various gaming franchises". The authenticity of the footage is hard to ascertain but it certainly looks the part.
The Perfect Dark footage includes the bare-bones layouts of some level environments, a little gunplay testing (this looks to be particularly early), a couple of abilities, and even a few pieces of destructible fruit. Delicious.
LEAKED | Perfect Dark — 2 mins of GameplayPerfect Dark is a cancelled first-person shooter game that was under development by The Initiative and Crystal Dynamics pic.twitter.com/w5adSFPFem
The reboot of Rare's Perfect Dark series was first announced back in December 2020, and was in development at new Xbox Game Studios developer The Initiative. The game became infamous for its slow and seemingly difficult development, with Tomb Raider developer Crystal Dynamics at one point recruited to help with it. In May 2024, reports suggested "little meaningful progress" had been made since the game's unveiling and that the reboot was in "a very rough state".
We got our first trailer for the Perfect Dark game just after that report, however, which seemed to reignite belief in the project. Alas, one year later, reports of its demise began to circulate. The game would have reportedly taken on an episodic structure, and after its cancellation, there was a suggestion that Take-Two might have snapped up the rights to the game, but this apparently fell through.

item.title: The Coalition, the Microsoft-owned studio behind Gears of War: E-Day, Gears 4 and Gears 5 has mostly survived the wide-ranging cuts and layoffs initiated by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in her attempt to bring the gaming division back to profitability. Read more
item.description:
The Coalition, the Microsoft-owned studio behind Gears of War: E-Day, Gears 4 and Gears 5 has mostly survived the wide-ranging cuts and layoffs initiated by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma in her attempt to bring the gaming division back to profitability.
But as Eurogamer reported, now that Gears of War: E-Day has shipped, many within The Coalition fear they're going to be laid off shortly afterwards, potentially missing out on bonuses.
Now, in an interview with the BBC, studio head Mike Crump was asked about the report and whether cuts are planned for the Canadian studio. Crump didn't offer specifics about the future of the studio, however.
"What I say to myself, what I say to the team, is we just we need to focus on the things that we can control," said Crump. "For us that's about shipping a great game that people are going to love and I feel like, as a team, we've done that."
E-Day has been fairly well-received by critics and embraced by players, boasting the series' best numbers on Steam. In the Eurogamer E-Day campaign review, Dom Peppiatt said the game proves there's still life left in the aging franchise.
But the big question is whether that is going to be enough to keep The Coalition safe and convince Xbox to invest in a future project. E-Day is an Xbox console exclusive - a decision reportedly hastily made just before the game's big summer reveal - which limits its audience and sales potential.
"Gears has been an exclusive franchise to Xbox for 20 years now. It's sort of entwined deeply with the brand," said Crump.
Asked how the studio measures success, the studio head said that while numbers are important, there's more that gets taken into account. Said Crump, "We measure things like, are we showcasing the platform? Are we pushing the hardware to its limits? Are we showcasing what the Xbox is capable of?
"Our goal basically is to be the best-looking game on the Xbox and really show the industry what's possible with our hardware."
After shipping Gears 5 in 2019, it took The Coalition seven years to develop and release Gears of War: E-Day. To that end, the studio boss believes E-Day makes for a "great foundation" for future sequels, and promises the next game "will not take nearly as long" to develop. The Coalition has not announced any future projects.
